speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the government have given this matter a great deal of attention, having had the salaries of the postal employees carefully considered by two bodies. On the Orders of the Day:

Mr. Speaker, I beg to draw the
attention of the Prime Minister to an editorial which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of May 29, 1924, as to the standing of the High Commissioner of Canada in London, in the course of which it is stated:
An interview between a high commissioner and a minister of the British government requires a good deal of arrangement, and not infrequently has proved impossible, the high commissioner being politely referred to subordinate officials, and such a thing has been known to happen even to ministers of the Canadian government present in London on various missions.
And further on is the following:
If a Dominion high commissioner has business to transact with a member of the British government, he should have access, by appointment if necessary, to the minister in question, and it is a strange thing indeed if such access is denied. The high commissioner's official status may be relatively low, but he is the highest permanent representative of his government, and as such he should be treated.
I would ask the government if these are true statements of fact, and, if so, is the government seeking a remedy?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There have been occasions I think, when the high commissioner has found it difficult to obtain interviews with British ministers, but the latest communications I have had from him would indicate that the British government are doing their best to accommodate him in this respect.

Pulpwood Commission
The question of the status of the high commissioners is being considered by the British government at the present time. When the former Secretary of State for the Colonies left office he had made certain recommendations with respect to the precedence to be given the high commissioners. Naturally the matter has been referred to his successor, and I understand that the British government are not yet in a position to make an official public announcement as to what will be ultimately arranged, but that they hope to do so in the very near future.

Hon. J. A. ROBB (Acting Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 173, to amend The Trust Companies Act, 1914.
Trust Companies Act

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 1-Specified securities, proviso.

It will be observed that the
proviso is underlined. This provision was previously subsection 9 of the section and has been transferred to paragraph (c) of subsection 1 to make clearer its meaning.

What is the idea of the minister in connection with section 1, in a case like this, for example:	The companies are authorized to invest trust furds in such securities as are authorized by the terms of trusts; but supposing you have a trust which is silent as to the character of the investments-that is not uncommon among people who do not understand them-what is the situation then?

They would have to invest in
trustees' securities.

What section
says that?
Section 63 of the act.
Is that in this act or in the old act? What does the old act say?

Section 63 provides:
(1) The company may invest trust money in,-
(a)	the debentures, bonds, stocks or other securities of or guaranteed by the government of the Dominion of Canada; or of or guaranteed by the government of any province of Canada, or of or guaranteed by the government of the United Kingdom, or of any colony or dependency thereof; or of or guaranteed by the government of the United States or of any state thereof; or of any municipal or school corporation in Canada; or guaranteed by any municipal corporation in Canada; or secured by rates or taxes, levied under the authority of the government of any province of Canada on property situated in such province and collectable by the municipalities in which such property is situated; or
(b)	first mortgages or hypothecs upon improved freehold real estate in Canada; or
(c)	such securities as are authorized by the terms of the trust: Provided, however, that, notwithstanding the terms of any trust, the company shall not invest or lend money deposited with the company in trust for investment, in respect of which the payment of interest or the repayment of principal is guaranteed by the company, in or upon the security of securities other than those authorized by subsections one and three of section sixty-six of this Act.
This latter proviso I have read is the amendment we now propose.
That is the only amendment? I thought perhaps the first was also an amendment.
That is old.
So, really all that is new is the proviso. The proviso seems to be a step in the right direction.

My hon. friend himself had
that proviso in the act.

I thought it
was the old law. so really there is no change in the law, and this is simply putting the act in more readable shape, is that the idea?
Yes.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-No loans to directors.
Is that new?

It is new so far as trust funds
are concerned.

I see by the note that
this is an adaptation of the limitation upon funds of insurance and loan companies, but if we are going to do this thing, why not do it well while we are at it? This provides that the company shall not lend trust funds to any of its directors, or to the wife or any child of any of its directors. What an ingenious directorate in necessitous circumstances may easily discover is a father or mother. Very often the speculative period of life is in the younger days, and I can understand some young Napoleon of finance whose father or mother is still living calling him or her in aid as a recipient of the loan. Why not embody the Levitical degrees generally in this, and make it broad enough so that no reasonably near relative of a director shall receive any money? Simply to say wife or child does not go far enough, it seems to me.

There is always a limit when
you are imposing restrictions, and we have not heard of any abuse in the direction in-' dicated by my hon. friend. We put in this clause to cure some abuses that have already been discovered. We must draw a line somewhere in imposing restrictions.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-Differing provisions repealed.

I think perhaps
we had better know what we are going to cut out.

This is to remove some of the restrictions that are considered unreasonable. The subsection repealed reads as follows:
Any provision in any special act or elsewhere conferring upon any company any other or wider powers of loaning or investment than those conferred by this act is hereby repealed.

Trust Companies Act

Just what are these restrictions that are being: removed? Is the minister satisfied that they have not constituted, after all a bargain between the investors and the company itself? They may be intended as a part of the charter for the protection of those loaning or investing money. They may have desired these restrictions. I am in ignorance and the committee is in ignorance, and I think we ought to have a statement of the character of these restrictions and the companies to which they apply.

There is, for instance, a restriction contained in section 67 of the Companies Act which is made applicable to certain companies by their special acts, and which prohibits the company from loaning any of its funds to any shareholder. It is believed this restriction is unnecessarily severe. My hon. friend will observe that section 3 prohibits a company from investing or lending any of its funds on the security of its own stock, but there does not seem to be any reason for prohibiting loans to shareholders on other satisfactory security.

Section agreed to.
On section 5-Superintendent to ascertain expense of administration of act during last preceding fiscal year.
I do not remember discussing this before.

We discussed this on the
resolution.

Is the idea
there of arriving at the amount of income for the purpose of rateably charging the companies with the expenses?
Yes.

I suppose the
thing will work out this way. It will be an open question until the end of the year how the cost will be distributed. The principle running through the whole thing, I suppose both as to these and the loan companies, will be to apportion the cost to each company in the ratio that their reasonable incomes bear to such cost-is that the idea?
That is right.

Section agreed to.
On section 6-Consideration of sale may be shares in stock of purchasing company.
Sir HENRY DRAY'TON:	I was just going to ask the minister whether this follows
the usual form or not. Of course, there is not much use in giving the right of sale or amalgamation to these companies unless the stock provision is put in; there is no doubt about that. This or a similar provision ought to be enacted. The usual provision is that the company shall have power "to sell and dispose of the whole or any part of the business, rights and property of the company, for such consideration as the company may think fit-"and then the shares, debentures or securities of any other company, having objects altogether or in part similar to those of the company." I suppose the position is that this clause does exactly the same thing.
It permits the selling company to take shares in the purchasing company.

Why is the provincial company a trust company within the meaning of the Dominion act? Is there a clause in the Dominion act extending this to provincial companies? That is the only query that suggests itself to me.

We are putting in this provision to make sure. I read from chapter 55:
Company or trust company incorporated for the purpose of-
The definition does not say whether it is incorporated by the Dominion or by the provincial authorities. The understanding of the department is that it means any company.

Would it not
be clearer if we were to say: "In any sale under the authority of this section of the whole of the business, rights and property of the trust company."

Well, "company" means trust
company by the interpretation section.
Sir HENRY DRAY'TON:	Supposing we
insert 'the word " trust." Would that cover the whole thing and make it perfectly clear?
We will consent to putting the word "trust" in, it will not do any harm.
All right. It makes the meaning clearer, I think

I submit there is a constant, persistent, insidious attempt on the part of the departments of government here -and it does not matter what government is in power-to encroach upon provincial rights. I do not believe that this parliament has the slightest authority to pass such legislation in regard to a provincially incorporated trust
Trust Companies Act

company doing business in its own province. Nevertheless we are eternally getting into conflict, and going into the courts, to find out whether we can possibly extend our jurisdiction. If the jurisdiction of parliament is to be revised let it be revised by reconsideration of the British North America Act and a new definition of our powers. If the provinces have come to a point where they are willing that that should be done, let them say so; but until that time comes why should we pass legislation that is absolutely futile, and just as misleading as it is futile?

Does not my hon. friend
observe that under this legislation we permit a Dominion company to sell out to a provincial company?
I had not observed that.

Yes, we are making that
provision.

There is an amendment to be made. I propose that the word "trust" be placed after the word "any" on the third line.

Mail Subsidies and Steamship Subventions-Canada and the West Indies and South America, or both, service or services between, $340,666.66.

I would ask the minister to let this one item stand for the present. There are several members engaged at the present moment on the Banking
committee who, I know, wish to query the minister in connection with the item and to discuss it.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. LOW (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
I would be very glad indeed to
oblige the hon. member, but I have been especially asked to bring on this one item first, because some members who would like to discuss it will not be here this evening.

The meeting of the Banking committee was almost inevitable to-day, and I think perhaps the minister could meet the convenience of both those who desire to leave this evening and those who wish to speak on this item. It is just this one item I refer to.
Why not let these gentlemen speak who desire to, and then hold the item over?

Very well. The subsidy of
$340,666.66 is the same as in previous years. In 1920 we entered into an agreement with the West Indian government which provided for a service between Canada and the Islands, and a clause was inserted that the government of Canada would use its best endeavours to arrange for a mail, passenger, and freight steamship service to come into effect as soon as possible, and in any case within three years, between Canada, Bermuda, the Leeward Islands, Barba does, Trinidad, and British Guiana. In 1921 tenders were called for, and a contract was given to the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company. That contract expired in 1923, when another call was made for tenders. There was only one tender received, that of the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company, at an increased rate, $584,000. We carried on negotiations for some little time and finally agreed to renew the contract for one year at the former subsidy of $340,666.66 odd. During the year we hope to look into the matter and try, if possible, to secure a better service, even supposing we have to pay a slightly increased subsidy. Our trade with the WTest Indies is increasing very rapidly, and I think this is one service upon which the money would be well spent.

I desire to take up the time of the House at perhaps a considerable length for this stage of the session, but if my remarks are lengthy, my excuse is the supreme importance of this whole question of our trade with the West Indies.
Under this item I think it is well for us to discuss, as business men, just where we stand with reference to this whole West Indian matter. The average Canadian, I am
Supply-Steamship Services

afraid, thinks of the West Indies-by which I mean that part of America which touches the Caribbean sea; in addition to Demerara, and British Honduras, an area of over 190,000 square miles, with a population of nearly nine millions of people-as countries low in purchasing power, needing and purchasing the necessaries of life in a very limited degree. Indeed, this is not only the idea of Canadians at home, but true of many of those who have visited the islands of the West Indies and who have come back with the story there is no purchasing power there worth while.
In connection with this vote, which is for steamship communication with these islands, I desire to put before this House and the country some figures which I think will impress them with the great importance of this market, and the great purchasing power of these people. Let me say, shortly, that nearly everything they produce we need, and nearly everything they need we produce. I am going to put on Hansard what I have headed, Startling Facts Re West Indian Trade, putting the matter in a sort of tabloid form so that at a glanice we can judge something of the importance of the trade and perhaps of some of the mistakes that have been made in the past.
These are the facts which I submit are somewhat startling:
1. The total trade of the United States with the West Indies in 1923 amounted to $814,703,262, while the total trade of Canada with the West Indies, in spite of the fact that many of them are under our flag and have a preference with us, amounted during the fiscal year ending March 31, 1923, to only $54,999,429.
2.	The percentage of increase in United States trade in 1923 over 1922 was over 38 per cent; the increase in Canada's trade was less than 8 per cent.
3.	Sales by the United States to the West Indies in 1922-and this shows something of the purchasing power of these people,- amounted to $239,535,021, and in the follow-ng year, 1923, that had increased to $331,274,785, an increase in the trade of the United States with these countries, in one year, of $91,739,764.
4.	Dealing with Canada. The sales by Canada to the West Indies for the year ending March 31, 1922, amounted to $18,784,364. The sales by Canada to the West Indies for the year ending March 31, 1923, amounted to $19,406,333, or an increase in the year of only $621,969, as compared with an increase in the United States sales of $91,739,764.
[Mr. LoganJ
5.	Purchases by the United States from the West Indies in 1922 amounted to $350,970,640. Purchases by the United States from the West Indies in 1923 amounted to $483,428,475, or an increase in one year of $132,457,835.
6.	Canadian purchases from the West Indies in 1922 amounted to $31,532,461. Canadian purchases from the West Indies in 1923 amounted to $35,592,096, an increase of $4.059,635.
7.	Total increase in United States trade, ohat is imports and exports in 1923 over 1922 -and I think this is somewhat startling- was more than $224,000,000. Canada's trade during the same year increased about four and a half millions.

May I ask
the hon. member a question?

I would prefer being allorved to place this statement on Hansard before being interrupted. My hon. friend can put his question later.
8.	The United States has 70 consular agents in the West Indies and in the countries around the Caribbean Sea, who are really trade agents; Canada has but two trade agents in all that vast territory.
9.	Canada lost in operating the government ships, that is the ships of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, in the three years 1921, 1922 and 1923, an average of about $265,000 a year.

In the operation of the ships
on that route?

In the operation of Canadian Government Merchant Marine ships on the West Indian route. I will give some details of this in a moment. Incidentally, we paid to the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company the amount which we are asked to vote again to-day, the sum of $340,666.66 a year to compete with the line that was losing already at the rate of $265,000 a year.
10.	Canada buys yearly about $100,000,000 worth of tropical products from the United States, many of which are imported by that country from the West Indies. These products from the West Indies are carried to American ports by American vessels, and over American railways, to a point nearest the Canadian consumption, while we pile up deficits on our Government Merchant Marine and on our National Railways. For instance, last year Canada imported over 2,000,000 stems of bananas, and only 23,000 of these came into this country direct. Canada imported from the United States in 1923 over

Supply-Steamship Services
iS,000.000 pounds of grapefruit and only 400000 pounds came into this country from the West Indies direct.
13.	Here is a very startling statement. It has been submitted to me and I have every reason to believe it is quite correct. It would require 56 trains of 40 cars of 40 tons each to transport Canadian imported tropical products from Canadian ports to the points of Canadian consumption. Yet- all that business is going over American lines. For instance if these fruits are bought in Winnipeg they come in through the city of New York being transported thereto by American ship, through an American port, through American brokerage films, put on American railroads, and carried probably to an American railway point within sixty or seventy miles of Winnipeg.
14.	Another startling statement is: According to the average rate of exchange of last year Canada lost nearly $2,000,000 in exchange on tropical products purchased from the United States. Why should Canada not use this money which at present is absolutely thrown away as far as this country is concerned in providing cold storage facilities on Canadian ships? Why not employ more trade agents to secure increased trade direct to Canada?

May we
take the trade figures the hon. gentleman has given as being the total trade to the West Indies, or do they refer simply to the British West Indies?

When I commenced my remarks I explained that when I referred to the West Indies I meant all the islands that are washed by the Caribbean Sea and in addition British Honduras and Demerara.
Any true Canadian is bound to ask the question: What is the remedy for this condition of affairs? Why is it that the United States of America enjoy a trade with a country which is almost foreign to them, except Porto Rico, of over $800,000,000, while Canada has but a trade of $54,000,000. What is the remedy? Well, I humbly submit, the first remedy is better steamship service. Mark you, I am not here to say that this vote should not pass. Under the circumstances I think the minister has done the right thing to continue the vote for one year in order that he may be able to look into this matter more thoroughly. But surely, we can devise some better means of carrying on this trade than paying one company $340,000 a year, whilst we are losing on our own service-which is calling at the same ports in the West Indies-the sum of $265,000 annually. Mark you, the pre-requisite for success in
transporting tropical fruit is cold storage- everybody knows that. I hold in my hand the agreement between the government and the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company which has been renewed year after year. There is not one single mention made in that contract of cold storage. Yet it is the one thing that is required, the one thing we must have, if we are going to carry tropical fruits for any great distance. I have gone over the contract rather thoroughly, and there are some features of it which seem to be a little weak. If we are going to renew the contract these parts should be strengthened. We do not provide for any speed whatever. Clause 8 reads:
The contractors bind themselves to run each of the four steamships hereinbefore referred to at their best speed.
That Coes not amount to very much. I do not know what their best speed would be. It might be 10 knots an hour.
The treaty calls for 11 knots.

There is a speed limit of 10
knots an hour.

I do not like to dispute with the minister. I would be glad if someone would point out to me the clause where the contract provides for any speed whatever per hour. Let me read the whole clause, and perhaps it will explain the matter. It is headed: "Rates of speed". It reads:
The contractors bind themselves to run each of the four steamships hereinbefore referred to at their best speed in the performance of the service herein contracted for, unless the speed of the ship is delayed by reason of stress of weather, or by assisting ships in distress, in any of which events the contractors shall submit to the minister the captain's explanation of the cause of the delay or such other evidence as the minister may require to enable him to determine, and the minister upon such explanation and evidence shall determine whether the circumstances were such as justified the captain's reduction of the speed of the voyage or sufficiently explain the delay in completing the voyage.
That is the end of the clause referring to the speed of the ships. But let us pass from these boats of the Royal Mail line. As I have said I am not here to condemn this line. I think they are carrying on under difficulties. They have not the proper provision made for the trade; at the same time they have done some excellent work in developing trade in that part of the world. We have the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, with four steamers running from Halifax to Bermuda, thence on to St. Kitts, Antigua, Barbadoes, and Trinidad, and on down to Demerara. On

Supply-Steamship Services
the other side, on the other leg of the Caribbean sea-that is towards the western islands-we have two ships, the Canadian Fisher and the Canadian Forester.
For some years we dickered with the people of the British West Indies in reference to their tmde agreement; and finally in 1920 an agreement was signed. I have in my hand a copy of that agreement, and I have no hesitation in saying-though I am perhaps speaking against what might be the contention of the department of the government-we are violating that agreement every day.
Some bon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.

And I will show hon. members how. In the first place we undertook, referring to the steamship service of the eastern group, to put on a line of steamers capable of maintaining an ocean speed of 12 knots an hour. I deny that these ships are there, or that they maintain that service. The clause reads:
The steamers shall be from 5,000 to 6,000 tons gross, capable of maintaining an ocean speed of 12 knots and providing accommodation for 100 first-class, 30 second-class and 100 steerage or deck passengers.
I deny that that accommodation is there, or that it is provided. Dealing with the steamship service for the western group- that is the group around by Jamaica-the contract provides that the steamers
-shall have an ocean-going speed of not less than 10 knots.
I have travelled on one of those boats within the last six months, and I can speak from experience. I was told by a person who knew that we did not average over seven knots an hour on a greater part of the journey. Imagine trying to operate a passenger service in this up-to-date world with steamers not making more than seven knots an hour.

When my hon. friend is
speaking about ships, is he referring to the Canadian Merchant Marine line or to the Royal Mail Steam Packet line?
I am now referring to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. There is another provision in this agreement which I will submit to my hon. friend who has asked the question, who is a good lawyer-
Carried.

I will commend it to my
hon. friend's judgment as to whether he could draft any better clause if he desired 
to. evade responsibility. This clause states the ships shall be provided:
-so far as the traffic warrants, with cold storage if this can be secured with reasonable cost-
Mark how it is hedged around:
-as the traffic warrants, and if this can be secured with reasonable cost-
It reminds me very much of the old story they used to tell about the late President Grover Cleveland. When out duck shooting, he ran out of food. In the morning he said to. his cook:	"What are we going
to have for breakfast?" And the cook replied, "If we had some ham we would have ham and eggs, if we had the eggs." No cold storage has been provided up to this date.

Is that the agreement
between the Canadian government and the West Indies?
Could the hon. member tell us if those ships could be equipped with cold storage at any reasonable expense?

I cannot answer that question and I do not think the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) can answer it; but in my concluding remarks, one of the things which I am going to advocate is that, if we do not know, we should endeavour to find out. If we cannot operate these ships better than we are doing now, let us scrap them or give them away. There is no use in losing $265,000 a year for play-time. I am not here however to advocate that we should do away with the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. I believe there are some parts of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine which are very valuable, and while I believe the Canadian Government Merchant Marine service between Maritime Canada in the East and Maritime Canada in the West and the West Indies can be of great benefit, the kind of ships we have now are practically useless.
Referring again to the trade agreement, I understand, it was after a lot of dickering, we entered into trade arrangements with different islands. We arranged for certain preferences. Some islands give us a much greater preference than others. For instance, in Bermuda we get only 25 per cent preference and in the Bahamas, only 10 per cent preference. In Barbadoes, on the other hand, we get 50 per cent preference. I advocate to-day that we offer to establish absolute 'free trade between those countries and Canada. No protectionist can raise the question for a moment that there is any interference with any Canadian industry. There are no manufacturers there to compete with industries in this country. For a few years they have been under a certain degree of prosperity owing to some extent to the McKenna treaties under the British tariff. These McKenna treaties, as we all know, are now to be abrogated, and a psychological moment has arrived when the question is how long the patience of these islands is going to be maintained. I am rather shocked to find in an editorial in a leading paper known as the Canada-West Indian Magazine certain statements in reference to conditions as they exist now, showing the temper of the people. In the May issue of this magazine, I find the following:
To say that the dropping of preference by the Labour government in Great Britain has created profound disappointment throughout the overseas portion of the Empire is no exaggeration. The fact that the
Labour government's policy in this matter would seem to be endorsed by a very large proportion of the electorate, even of those who do not belong to the Labour party, is taken as indicating that for this generation at any rate imperial preference is a dead issue. Undoubtedly this marks a turning point in the history of the Empire. The dominions and colonies are now resigning themselves to the task of working out their own economic destinies without any special co-operation or assistance from the home country, and with the feeling that any preference they may now be giving to goods manufactured in Great Britain is in opposition to the principles of those who benefit by it, and therefore not held to be of any high value either in principle or effect. In the circumstances it is inevitable that the dominions and colonies will look elsewhere for the trade agreements and alliances upon which their economic structure will in future be founded.
It is pleasing to note that the first reaction to the home government's policy has been for the dominions and colonies to look to each other for such extension of trade agreements as will enable them to develop trade one with another, and thus to build up a British preference in which the only non-reciprocating portion of the Empire will be Great Britain. One instance of this is found in the negotiations now proceeding between Canada and Australia for an agreement which will give Australian commodities a preference in the Canadian market and place Canadian commodities on an equal footing with goods from Great Britain in the Australian market. Then again, there is renewed interest in the reciprocity agreement between Canada and the West Indies, and a disposition both in Canada and in the islands to still further develop the preferential policy.

If the economic tie is severed by a Labour govuument, it will probably also be severed by the various Colonial governments. That is the situation and it is just as well for us to face it squarely, for when we face it we Shall begin to think seriously of what to do in order to ensure a decent economic and industrial future for this country. I have listened with
intense interest, for the most part with approval, to all that has been said by both speakers of the afternoon. The significance

I do not wish to enter before six o'clock into any extended comment on either speech. These speeches consist of criticism in some degree of our past relations with the West Indies, and especially as to the manner in which we have carried out the trade agreement now subsisting, and as well of suggestions as to future means of intercourse and future regulations looking to an expansion of our trade. Let me express a feeling of regret that the speech of the minister should be open to the interpretation that a great blunder was made in the style of ship constructed for the merchant marine. I am not able at the moment to discuss the exact knottage per hour, the tonnage, or the cold storage and passenger facilities of the special boats running to the West Indies. Suffice it to say that all are well constructed of the kind they are, all are constructed of the design felt by our best experts to be suited for the purposes that they were then built to meet.
But I do listen with very considerable interest to the conversion to the view that now that we have National Railways, we must have a mercantile marine. It is not without some considerable consolation to me that I hear those who once reprehended viciously the building of any ships at all now reducing their allegation merely to the question of the character of ships built. All this is a step in the right direction, to use the expression of hon. gentlemen to my left. When we hear those who once said that as soon as the war was over we should have ceased building any vessels, we should have cancelled all contracts made, we should have gone out of a business in which we could not succeed, now saying that we must prepare our minds for the extension of the principle; that we must face the building of more ships of a faster and better kind, that is at least a reflection on much of the criticism that we heard during the last few years.

However, any proposal of that kind will receive fair consideration at our hands. We do not believe in extensions beyond what is required for such purposes as essentially must be served while the responsibility of railway management is upon us.
The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) proceeded to press not only for better ocean services to the West Indies but also for more effective trade regulations looking to the extension of trade with our fellow Britishers of the West Indies, and also-and this was more immediately in his mind-looking to the diversion of such trade as we have through the port of New York and over American railways to our own ports and over our own roads. I think all members will gladly get behind any proposals effective to that end. But I notice that some hon. members almost shudder when a suggestion is made, especially if it comes from across the way, that the trade regulation which would be effective in order to turn West Indian trade to our own ports, and at the same time tend to develop that tradd by giving it an advantage over other trade that is not nearly so beneficial to us, would be by the imposition of tariff duties against that other trade.

Tariff regulations are like any other regulations:	They can be used for more purposes

Well, I .did not know

Since I have sat in this House I have advocated closer trade relations with the West Indies. It was a source of great encouragement this afternoon to see four hon. members on their feet at once in their desire to speak on the subject following the remarks of the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) who so ably and enthusiastically handled the question. When I very humbly presented my views the first year I sat in parliament the only one who gave me any sympathy was Mr. F. H. Keefer, who had been in the West Indies, as the hon. member for Cumberland has been. I went over and interviewed him upon his return, and I must say that I have not yet met a person who has been in the West Indies who was not impressed with their wonderful trade possibilities.
It has been said this afternoon that this is the accepted time and the day of salvation. In olden times we used to say "Educate, legislate, eradicate." We hope in this case the great word will be consummate. There is no other territory that this great and glorious Dominion of ours can look to for a tropical trade except the West Indies. It is our last opportunity to develop trade with a country that has a tropical climate. I must confess that my ardour had been dampened somewhat by the way in which the House used to treat this question. I have advocated closer trade relations with the West Indies in railway trains and hotel rotundas, lobbies and wherever I have been. I have urged Canadians, when they want to go to a sunny clime, to go to the West Indies instead of to California or to the Atlantic states. I have met with success in my efforts in that direc-
tion only so far as my own family is concerned, and when they returned they have always had more to say for the West Indies than they ever had to say for California and other parts of the United States they had visited. We should get to know these people of the West Indies, and incidentally make money by trading with them. I am sure that Canada would be proud of any closer relations that developed with the West Indies. Harry 'Crow, a strong political unionist, has exhausted his strength and resources in writing booklets and sending pamphlets from one end of this country to the other. I also have the pleasure of taking the Cuiban-Canadian Magazine and reading it occasionally, I have seen what the great Macauley of the Sun Life Insurance Company has to say. He does not believe in political union, but in commercial union. 'I am a political unionist-
I thought you were a church unionist.

I am emphatically a
church unionist, I am also a political unionist and that embraces commercial union. I was very glad to see the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) supported in his remarks, not only on this side of the House, but by the right hon. leader of the opposition. I hope this will not be made a party question at all. It concerns the future of all Canada, and we should be a unit in doing what we can to help this country become what we hope to see it some day. Take any large development, the Hydro Electric, for instance; there is always a stage in its development when by the building of a small dam you could starve the enterprise of its power, and we have to go in for the thing largely, issue large credits and secure all the riparian and other rights to make the thing a success, and that takes the credit of the country. I would be willing to see this country extend her credit to bring West Indian trade.
How ridiculous it is that the United Fruit Company of the United States should be able to go down there and control these people! The hon. member for Cumberland has spoken of that cargo of bananas that was shipped to Montreal recently. The United Fruit Company got ahead with a trainload of bananas, and sold them so cheap that when the cargo arrived the people interested in the cargo lost money. Thirty-five years ago, and prior to that, Montreal was the greatest fruit market on the continent for a few months of the year. Fruit dealers came up here from

New Orleans and bought their fruit at auction on the open market in Montreal. These auctions lasted for weeks and weeks just after navigation opened. The great family of Vipond and other wealthy Montreal families all had connections in Kingston, Jamaica, and they have struggled in the face of adversity to build up a big trade. It only takes a few recurrences of such a thing as my hon. friend from Cumberland described to destroy a business of that kind, and the Yiponds went on until their resources were exhausted. The last time I talked with the dear old man he had just returned from Kingston. They have lost their money through the great nation to the south getting control.
We have good reason for treating the people of the West Indies well. Owing to the grand banking system we have in this country we have branches of our banks down there. We have also a merchant marine of 28 boats. I do not propose to go into that question tonight-neither to defend nor assail our merchant marine-but I say that we should live up to our agreements, whether of 1920, or prior to that or since, and all unite to develop our trade with these islands. I believe we have won the hearts of these people already. They do not like the tactics of the United States. In British Honduras the people were encouraged to grow bananas, and when the fruit was ready they called on the American boats, and the answer they received was: "Who told you to raise bananas?" and those bananas rotted where they grew.
Fruit is a household necessity in Canada, and we cannot produce fruit ourselves except during a few months of the year. Happily the fruit that we raise they do not raise, but for six months they can supply us with all the fruit and garden produce we need in this country. On the other hand, they want our manufactured goods, our flour, and other commodities. One country is the complement of the other in that respect. Nobody thought forty years ago that California and Washington would be raising the products they are to-day, but when they found they had the same soil and climate as the eastern Mediterranean country they started in to experiment, and now we all know what they can do. There will have to be, in my opinion, free trade with these islands, and high protection for a while against the United States. I do not feel that will antagonize the feelings of our Progressive friends, because it will mean that we shall get the products of those islands here more cheaply than we are getting them now. That is the idea. You can go down
the street now and buy bananas for 15 to 30 cents a dozen. Why? Because the United Fruit Company cut the price for the time being. Do you think that company will bring up any more cargoes to Montreal after the experience they have had? Not on your life! It is beneath our dignity to acknowledge that we are too effeminate, too sissified, and too pussy-footed to stand on our own feet.
More than half a century has elapsed since confederation and if we are so effeminate as to allow the conditions to prevail to which I have alluded I am very sorry. Now, I am just as ardently desirous of bringing Newfoundland into confederation as anyone could be. But for the unwillingness of the government of the late Sir Mackenzie Bowell to incur an obligation of $8,000,000 the union of Newfoundland with Canada would have been accomplished long ago. And that money even if it had been $18,000,000 would not have been thrown away. There would have been a return to Canada of far more than any such sum had Newfoundland entered confederation. The same thing can be said of any expenditure which may be necessary to bring about a closer union between Canada and the West Indies. The United States knows the value of the West Indian islands, and I am convinced that she would cancel Britain's entire debt to her if she could secure possession of those islands. If they became the property of the United States we should be at the mercy of that country in the matter of tropical products which are now so largely consumed in this Dominion. I believe that even cotton can be raised in the West Indian islands. Think what an advantage it would be to have a supply of this raw material in a British possession quite near our own doors. On one occasion I was visiting a town in my own county and spoke of the desirability of our having possession of the West Indies. This expression of opinion evoked from a most influential man, the publisher of a newspaper, the remark " What do we want of 15,000,000 niggers?" This indicates how little is known in Canada about conditions in the West Indies. As a matter of fact the entire population there is not one-fifth of 15,000,000. It seems to me that we spend too much time here in cavilling over petty questions to the neglect of really important issues. For my part I am most optimistic over the trade possibilities between Canada and the West Indies.

I listened with great interest to the speeches this afternoon, more particularly to the address of the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan). To tell the truth the hon. member has given us considerable food for thought. Basing his argument on the ground of patriotism and of Empire interest, indeed of national interest, he has seemingly made out a pretty good case. Equally with the hon. member I should like to see a line of our own boats in the service between Canada and the West Indies, but it would seem that the vessels of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine are not at all suited to the carrying of Canadian commerce. We were told last year that these ships could not be used in the Canadian cattle trade on the Atlantic because they were too small and otherwise not adapted for the purpose. Neither could they be used in the carrying trade on the Great Lakes because they were not suitable as grain boats. I hope the men who designed these ships for the Canadian government will not design any more vessels should we see fit to enlarge the present merchant marine. Finally the discussion to-day proved that the vessels referred to are not suitable for the West Indian trade. I think the advisers of the government at the time they were constructed certainly meant these boats to be a failure. Perhaps they were more interested in private ownership than in national ownership. If so that would partly account for the peculiarity of the design of these vessels.
While we would like to trade with the West Indies we have a great deal to consider before we build and equip the needed vessels, or otherwise foster trade through artificial means, even with that part of the Empire. I have yet to find out where any nationally subsidized lines of vessels have been a success. There was a time during the last century when the United States planned to drive British shipping off the seas, and heavily subsidized vessels of their own. To-day the British merchant marine still holds its place on the seas. Britain's maritime trade has been constantly increasing ever since the war, and it will not be long until the Mother Country regains her former place in the carrying trade of the world.
We might naturally expect that a trade of considerable extent would naturally develop between the West Indies and the eastern part of Canada. But it is very doubtful if sufficient trade, say to provide the rest of Canada fMr. Evans.]
with tropical products, could be successfully carried on through Canadian Atlantic ports. Even to put bananas coming from the West Indies on the free list, and to impose a trade penalty against the Americans, would be futile; the ports of the Maritime provinces are too far away from that part of Canada where the greatest market for tropical products exists. I refer to the grain belt of the three prairie provinces. It is a futile argument to advance that because we have the National Railways on our hands, running from Halifax to Vancouver, these railways must get this traffic, when it is economically impossible to land those tropical products where they are needed in the Dominion, even with a heavy trade penalty against competitors. The distance from the ports of entry to the place of consumption is too great.
Let us for a moment take a look at the contour of the Dominion and the position of the West Indian islands. A good part of those islands are just about as near to Vancouver as they are to Halifax, with a fine-navigable route at their disposal. When you land the products referred to at Vancouver you are over eleven hundred miles nearer the great grain belt of western Canada, the section where those products are really needed than is the case when importation takes place at Halifax. If the Hudson Bay railway were completed it would enable us to land these products in the very heart of Canada, near the place where they are mostly needed, with half the rail haul, even from Vancouver. The Hudson Bay railway would facilitate trade between Canada and the rest of the wrorld, as no other expenditure of a like-sum would do in any other way. The ports on that great inland sea should be developed, in preference to subsidizing a line of boats to carry on an artificially established trade between any part of the world and those-ports. This country should develop her natural channels of trade, rather than spend money to artificially develop ports that entail a land haul too great to be of any advantage. The experience in the past shows that it is a very serious matter to attempt to turn trade out of its natural channels.
We have on our hands to-day a railway problem of tremendous magnitude because of the fallacious policy that was insisted on years ago of keeping our trade going East and West. Sentiment and privilege have-played too great a part so far in the development of this country, and it has proved too costly. The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) says that we are afraid

The question before the
House is an item of $340,000 to subsidize the services between Canada and the West Indies and South America. I may say that since this principle of subsidizing mail service came into force many years ago the whole question of water-borne traffic has been revolutionized. In looking over these subventions and mail subsidies, I notice that some of them are granted from the opening of navigation to the close. Others are by contract with privately owned companies. Some of them are simply for a subsidy to the company and the company allows the government to regulate rates, carry the mail free and grants other concessions. In regard to this whole vote, I think the time has come for a change. Hon. gentlemen will notice that the amount is exactly the same as last year, $340,000 although the rates have been reduced. The operations of the boats have been curtailed, and many other matters that enter into and regulate ocean rates must be considered. The people of Canada have the key in their own hands. The principle of subsidizing these services was adopted by the government many years ago, and waterborne traffic was very largely assisted. In those days Canada did not have any National Railways, ocean services, merchant marine, or lake service. We did not have many other services which the National Railways provide to-day. The only nationally owned railway was the Intercolonial.
If you are going to adopt the principle of subsidizing the services to the West Indies and South America for the benefit of the people and parts of the Maritime provinces the system should be extended to the head of the lakes, in my opinion, because it has been shown by the evidence taken before the commission recently that there is a lake shipping combine on the lakes and an ocean shipping combine on the ocean. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) spoke of the merchant marine "sitting in" with the railways in fixing rates. What have we on the Atlantic seaboard
to-day? We have a combine not only in the United States but in Canada as to ocean services which combine is in league with the railways, and this combine keeps up the rates. The members of the combine sit around the table and determine what the rates shall be. Have hon. members ever considered if any money is thrown away in the subventions granted to these steamship services? There is a combine in the steamship service in Ontario and at the head of the lakes, and the monopoly has frozen out all competition in water-borne traffic. Canada has expended on railways, according to the figures submitted to the House by the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George (Mr. Marler) in his speech on the budget, two billion dollars, whereas little or nothing has been expended on facdi-ties for the carriage of water-borne traffic. This item of $340,000 is five per cent on $6,400,000 of capital, and here we are asked to grant a subsidy of $340,000. I agree with a great deal of what the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) said this afternoon. We frequently hear the plea "give the Canadian National Railways a chance" but we hardly ever hear any one say "give the merchant marine a chance." It would be far better if you gave the merchant marine a show, and you would not have to grant subsidies for this mail service. Why can the merchant marine not perform the functions which these boats perform? If hon. gentlemen will look into the history of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, they will see that it was the intention of the government that they should perform services for the Trade and Commerce department in conjunction with the railways, and in that way effect considerable economy. If hon. gentlemen look over the statement of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine on the Atlantic seaboard they will find that there is a deficit to-day, according to the last statement, of $9,368,000, of all charges including depreciation and interest. The main reasons for the decrease in operating deficit were the cancellation of South American, Mediterranean and certain other unremunerative services, also the curtailment as far as possible of general expenses.
The report further says:
Generally speaking full cargoes on outward trips were secured, but satisfactory cargoes were not obtainable for homeward trips, which naturally increased operating expenses out of all proportion to operating revenues.

The first vessel sailed from Halifax on January 25, 1921, with a full complement of passengers and a cargo of flour, potatoes, oats, cement and general merchandise.
It must be remembered in connection with this service that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine are pioneers in opening up a new route with a view to developing and extending Canada's trade. As it has been the practice of many governments to supplement the earnings of companies engaged in this work, and as steamship subsidies are paid by the Dominion government for services that are much more remunerative than this West Indies service, it would only be reasonable that your company should be guaranteed against loss when engaged, as in this case, in opening up a new route at the request of the government.
The report refers also to the freight service and return cargoes to South America. It states that all of the above are freight services and that the vessels on the Nassau, Kingston and Belize service have some passenger accommodation. It also states that regular cargo services are now established to points in the United Kingdom, to Australia and New Zealand, to the West Indies and to South America. I do not believe they 
have had a proper chance or can have a proper chance on account of the way in which they have been operated. If we expand the services and build some new fast steamships to take care of this traffic between Canada and the West Indies and South America as the Americans are doing to-day, that would be a good thing for the Maritime provinces and for the merchant marine and would act as a feeder for the National Railways. I admire the people of the United States. They have been rebuilding their merchant marine; they have been going out to the West Indies, down to South America and upon the seven seas, and to-day they are securing the trade. I should like to read from the National City Banks' Trade Bulletin of recent date, to show the way in which the United States' merchant marine to-day are working in conjunction with a great steam railway on the Atlantic seaboard in order to secure the trade for the United States. I will give the committee a comparison between the years 1913 and 1922, the last year of record, of the business done between the United States and) the West Indies and South America,, showing how trade has doubled. Argentina took 33 per cent of her total imports from the United States in 1920 as against 15 per cent in 1913. Brazil took 16 per cent of her total imports from the United States in 1913. In 1921 that had increased to 32 per cent. Chile in 1913 took 17 per cent from the United States. This increased to 32 per cent in 1923. Peru in 1913 took 28 per cent. This increased to 55 per cent in 1923. The same is true all the way down. The same is the case in connection with the West Indies. The United States has come out of the war with a great merchant marine. It is going out not only to the West Indies and South America, but to the seven seas of the world with its merchant marine and getting the trade. There is a field on the ocean and in 9 p.m. the West Indies as yet unexplored for the Canadian National Railways if they get proper, up-to-date ocean and lake services, not only to take care of the traffic which offers but to provide feeders for the railway in the same way as the United states merchant marine is building up the railways of that country.
There is also the question of the control of rates to be considered in connection with this vote. The minister has, I understand, in exchange for the subsidies the power to regulate the rates, and the boats carry the mails free. That principle of control should be extended at the head of the lakes. The

You have just to read those reports from cover to cover to see how the subsidy principle has been abused in the past, how the ships to-day are not earning the subsidies which they are being given and how some new system should be established by the department involving the utilization of government-owned ships. It would be a good policy for the Minister of Railways and Canals to bring down a vote in this House so as to have a proper lake and ocean service from the merchant marine and thus aid as a feeder the National Railways. It would be a bright day for the Maritime provinces if such a state of affairs were brought about. What is the object of spending all this money on harbours for the Maritime provinces if these merchant marine ships are to be sold? What is to become of the Canadian National Railways without up-to-date ocean services? Let us see what the Canadian Pacific, the competitor of the National Railways are doing. They started as a Tailway. They spread to ocean services, lake services, hotel services, land services, and to-day they are 'a great railway paying dividends to 140,000 shareholders in connection with services established on ocean and on land. To-day they are a success. Parliament is voting $28,000,000 for branch lines; we have spent nearly $2,000,000,000 on railway land services, and we have spent little or nothing on ocean services. How can these all be a success if they are half starved? Some of these boats are old boats, not properly fitted out. They should be re-built, some for ocean services and some for lake services. There should be cold storage facilities on the lake and ocean boats, and they should be able to take care of fast passenger, package freight and express business. In that way you can build up the ports of St. John and Halifax and all the other ports on the gulf and seaboard. Let us take a leaf out of the book of the United States, where the people have done something to capture the balance of trade of the West Indies and South America. We pay subsidies for the carriage of mail and package freight, but I think this policy has outlived its usefulness, and the sooner the government realize that every up-to-date railway system must have proper ocean services on the Atlantic seaboard, on the gulf and on the lakes the better it will be for the revenues of our National Railways. Ocean rates are now under the -control of nobody apparently. I do urge on the minister to have a proper survey made to see whether something cannot be done to rebuild, extend and broaden out our Canadian Government Merchant Marine and put it in a condition to be of real sendee to the country. Some of our boats can be rebuilt and made available for the traffic which we are now subsidizing. When we look over the list we are told that one boat is not fitted for this traffic, another is not fitted for that traffic-in a word we find that they are fitted neither for mail nor package freight traffic. Who is to blame for building ships of that class, what, if anything, are they fit for? I repeat, we should have a survey made, and whatever boats are not suitable should be altered and made available for the mail service and general freight purposes on lake and ocean for which we are now subsidizing private companies to the extent of $340,000, for the West Indian and South American route alone.
Why should our boats be put on routes all over the world which do not give an adequate return cargo? In the last ten or fifteen years to my own knowledge there has been an elaborate West Indies and South America exhibit at our Canadian National Exhibition to show the people of Canada what the West Indies and South America produce and how we can expand our trade with our fellow Britishers in the West Indies and with

Mr. Chairman, the development of our trade with the West Indian islands is the most important question from the Maritime standpoint that can be discussed this session. In fact, I would not be exaggerating if I said that the solution of this problem is almost vital to the provinces down by the sea. Owing to certain reasons, which I need not state, the Maritime provinces are shut off from trade with our neighbours to the south except to a very limited extent. The only countries we can trade are with the West Indian islands and Great Britain; we cannot trade with central Canada except in a one-sided way. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) has so well covered the ground that very little more need be said. My remarks will apply to the Maritime provinces generally and to Prince Edward Island in particular.
The farmers in central Canada can supply, and more than supply, the food requirements of the cities in these parts, and no matter what the freight rates may be we cannot enter this market to any considerable extent. In fact the farmers of this part of the Dominion and farther west enter the small market that we have in St. John, Halifax and the Sydneys and compete with us. Now, the West Indian islands lie close to us as far as transportation rates are concerned, for water-borne commerce is the cheapest in the world. They require nearly everything that we produce, except, I presume, coal; our butter, our cheese, our eggs, our fish, our hay, our grain, our potatoes, our lumber find a market there; and in turn we want what they produce. Therefore the trade seems to be a natural exchange, and anything that can be done to foster and develop it will enure to the advantage of both countries. For the reasons that I have mentioned confederation has never been, and never can be, of any advantage to the Maritime provinces and un-
less we can get compensation by developing our trade with the West Indian islands, we obtain no return for our contribution to the general fund.
These are the reasons why the provinces by the sea have not progressed with the rest of Canada. We have many natural resources; our people are industrious and they compare in intelligence, I think, with the people of other parts of Canada. But we are handicapped by our geographical position. We can never be a manufacturing centre and compete with the manufacturers in this part of Canada, because our power would be derived from coal, which cannot compete in price with the electric power developed from the immense water powers of Ontario and Quebec. The extent to which cheap electric power can be developed in those two provinces gives them an advantage that no other part of Canada possesses, except, perhaps, British Columbia, and it is an advantage which, I should think, ought to enable them to meet all reasonable competition without their asking for any considerable aid through a tariff. With these great natural advantages, Ontario and Quebec ought to be in a fair way to meet the competition of the world. So it is vital to us, if we are to maintain our place at all, that this West India market shall be developed. I was more than pleased this afternoon to hear the Minister of Railways say that the matter was receiving the serious attention of the government and. that the business men of the Maritime provinces would be called into consultation with the government and the officials of the department to devise the best methods that could be followed. That is certainly the proper course to pursue and it will necessarily bring results.
Just a word in regard to trade commissioners, a matter which was referred to by the hon. member for Cumberland. From a question asked by an hon. member on the other side I gathered that he thought the government should not incur the expense of sending trade commissioners there, but that the cost of anything in that line should be borne by the people engaged in the trade. There may be something to be said for that, but in the initial stages I think the government would have to send some trade commissioners. This, however, is the point I make, and I think it will appeal to every member of the committee: if we send trade commissioners at all they ought to be the most suitable men for that purpose who can be found. There is very little use in sending young, inexperienced men to those places. Whatever professional men or men trained in the law

may think of it, no business man would entertain the idea for a moment no matter how intelligent they may be, these young men have not had the experience, and nothing can take the place of experience in trade matters. The very best trade commissioners would be men who have actually been engaged for some years in the business of import and export, men who have traded with these islands, men who naturally know the business and have had the experience. It does not matter how old they are; the older the better, provided they are active and able to do their work. If the Civil Service Act will not permit that to be done, I should think parliament would be willing to pass a measure giving to the Department of Trade and Commerce the right to appoint trade commissioners. When Mr. Breadner, a former member of the staff of the Customs department, was some years ago placed at the head of the Income Tax branch, being a practical man he stipulated that he be allowed to appoint his own men, and parliament gave him that power. He wanted practical men in that service and he determined that if they were to be appointed by the Civil Service Commission he would not take charge of that department. Of course the Civil Service Commission do not appoint the officials of the railways or of the merchant marine. In saying this I make no reflection whatever on the Civil Service Commission; very likely they are able to select suitable men for some branches of the service where education and intelligence are the chief requirements and where technical experience does not count for so much. But in this branch of the service nothing will take the place of actual practical experience, and every business man in Canada, I think, will endorse that statement. This matter is of great importance, and I am sure that the House would be willing to make any change by way of enactment that might be necessary to bring about the desired end in this respect.
There is little more to be added to the very able presentation of the ease by the hon. member for Cumberland and to the really pregnant statement made by the Minister of Railways. I think the views which I have presented are in accordance with the business view, and I trust that the matter will not be allowed to rest but that it will be taken up and proceeded with in order to obtain results quickly.

I had not the
advantage of being in the House this afternoon while the discussion was on, but I have 199
heard some of it to-night and I have also heard references made to what was said this afternoon. I know of no question of greater importance to the people of Canada than the extension of its services by sea for the expansion of our trade. The greatest example of success in the way of transportation in the world to-day is found in the National Railways owned by the people of Canada. There is nothing like it in the way of solving the transportation problem. The question of profits for shareholders has been eliminated and the whole problem has resolved itself into an attempt to give service at cost and to expand that service wherever possible. We do not quite realize here how successful that has been. It has made the rival of the Canadian National lines, the Canadian Pacific, see they are up against something they never thought would happen. They thought the old Intercolonial was to continue; they thought the old Grand Trunk was to continue; they thought that all the privately owned roads we had in this country would continue, and that they would have an easy chance perhaps to beat them out. But the amalgamation of these roads and the success of the Canadian National Railway has put the Canadian Pacific up on its toes.
Now, if we have succeeded, and we have succeeded, in connection with the Canadian National Railways, why should we not begin to apply that same principle to the handling of lake and ocean services? Why not expand the principle of public ownership a little, and let the management of the Canadian National Railways have in their charge transportation by water, whether by lake or by sea, as well as transportation by rail? If we did that we would then have a service by rail, a sea service, and a lake service, the whole underlying principle of which would be service at cost, service without profit for the Shareholders. That principle has proven so successful in connection with our railway that there should be no doubt of the success of its application to water transportation, either by lake or by sea. I would be prepared to do this, although I know the Canadian Pacific would not accept it: I think the Canadian Pacific might well consider whether the time had not come for them to consolidate perhaps in some way with the Canadian National Railway as far as railway transportation is concerned, and perhaps they would turn over their lake and sea service to a national transportation organization which would apply not only to land traffic but to water traffic as well. That may be rather an advanced idea to sug-

gest, but something like that has to be worked out.
If you read the papers as I have been reading them the last few days, you will see that the greatest monopoly that exists today is the combination that exists in lake and sea traffic. The whole of our lake traffic is controlled by one company, and the sea traffic is largely controlled by combines. If you want evidence of this take up one of the Winnipeg papers of this week, in which the farmers are told that it will be necessary for the government of this country to take up the question of ocean transportation. The farmers of the West can raise any amount of live stock now, and they could supply the whole meat requirements of a large proportion of Europe if they could only get low transportation rates by sea; but they cannot get them. As was pointed out by the Winnipeg Free Press this week, it costs 820 to transport a live bullock from an Atlantic port to a British port. There is no reason why Canada should not engage in sea traffic in the same way that she has in railway traffic, and get a few vessels to begin with to transport the live stock products of the Canadian West across the ocean. I am sure they would be able to bring the rate down from $20 to $10, and make money at that rate. But this frightful combination to keep up rates by sea rules the whole business, and has destroyed the prospects of the people of the west, and I would ask my Progressive friends to urge upon the government that they should take up this question.
We must go a step further in dealing with transportation than we have gone already. We must go to the point of dealing with transportation by sea, and if we do that and combine our public ownership of water transportation with our public ownership of land transportation, we will begin to get the leadership in the commerce of the world. There is more hope of that in combining those services than in anything else. We cannot do it in a one-sided way; we must take the two together, land and water transportation. We have to solve the question of transportation as it is applied to the sea as well as to the land, and if we do that we will make some headway, and hold out some hope of improving conditions in the Maritime provinces. There is no reason why we Should not, at a very small expense, employ the organization of the Canadian National railways to develop transportation by water, by a line of boats owned by Canada and running to the West Indies, to South America, and across the Atlantic, going into

the business in a small way to start with, in connection with transporting Canadian farm products, including live stock. I would trust Sir Henry Thornton to-morrow with ten million dollars, if he wanted it, to start a fleet of boats in connection with the Canadian National Railways, to run to the West Indies, to South America, and to give a service on the Atlantic ocean, a freight service to begin with, and especially for live stock. I have no doubt that if that experiment were made, we should make good. It would have to be tested by the cold facts. I was glad to hear the Minister of Railways hold out this afternoon some encouragement of an effort in that direction. You have to try it out, and my friends from the Maritime provinces and hon. members from the west are in a position to demand from the government that this be done.
The management of the Canadian National Railways has been so successful that it has carried consternation into the minds of railway owners all over the world. The Canadian people are behind the Canadian National Railways in the matter of train service; they have no doubt now as to the future; they know that there are Canadians who can run a railway successfully. The Canadian Pacific can do it, and so can the people who run the Canadian National Railways. The railways have made good, and1 I suggest to the members from the Maritime provinces and the members from the West that they get together and make it part of their programme right here and now that the National Railways shall be authorized to go into transportation by sea, in a small way to begin with, which will develop the ports and trade of the Maritime provinces, and help the farmers of the West by giving them cheap transportation for their grain, and especially for their cattle. If they do that, we will be in a position to show that Canada has solved the transportation problem in a way that no one else has solved it, by the application of public ownership to a combination of transportation by rail and by sea. That is what the transportation profiteers to-day are afraid of. They want to keep these things in private hands, and they have it in private hands in the matter of sea transportation, which is the greatest monopoly in the world to-day. There is nothing like it; the richest men and the richest combinations in the world to-day are those that control transportation by sea, and the way for Canada to develop and expand her trade is to follow the example we have in the Canadian National Railways and go into the business of transportation by sea on a small scale to begin with. Let us

I will put the leader of the opposition at ease. I do not intend to support any shipbuilding programme which will cost this country money; but I say that every year there are hundreds of thousands of ships which are ready at any time to carry the products of Canada to foreign lands. Do I understand my hon. friend to say that at the present time there is an overplus of bottoms throughout the world? Because if so I cannot understand why we are called upon to pay double rates on our cattle from here to the Old Country.

I have no hesitation in saying that the trade follows the flag, and that ships will go wherever the trade is. Wherever there is business for ships to do, ships will be found to carry all the business that is moving. What did my hon. friend from Cumberland say this afternoon? He spoke of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine coming up from the West Indies with 50 tons of freight, when it could have carried 3,000 tons, and he spoke of the Royal Mail Packet steamships coming up from the West Indies without any cargo. I was on the Hudson river about three weeks ago and saw 2,000 ships tied side by side upon that great majestic stream, and yet my hon. friend asks me if there is sufficient tonnage to d'o the business.
I asked the hon. member, if that were the case, how he explained the fact that rates were at an exorbitant figure at the present time as applied to some lines of industry?

That was the condition under the late government, and under this government as well, although perhaps neither the former government nor this government can be blamed for it, because in my opinion the mistake was made when the Canadian Government Merchant Marine ships were built
and a bill was passed in this House incorporating a company called the Canadian Government Merchant Marine Limited. A board of directors was appointed, which board was absolutely irresponsible to the owners of the ships, and they were given complete power to carry on the business of the ships, but the fact remains that the management of these boats, instead of endeavouring, as the hon. member would hope, and as I would hope, to keep down the rates on cattle or anything else, entered into a combine. The freight managers or directors of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine entered into a combine, not once or twice, but seven or eight times, not only to keep the rates up but to increase the rates on different products which were to be handled. My hon. friend must remember that the special committee on Agriculture last year went into that question and found that there was a combine. I proved to my own satisfaction two years before that there was a combine. If my hon. friend will read Hansard he will see that in my speech condemning the Canadian Government Merchant Marine I showed that they entered into an agreement known as the New York pool. I could mention another thing to show the way business was conducted by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. I think three years ago the manager of the Royal Mail Packet line came to Ottawa to interview the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The vessels of that company, as hon. members know, plied between Halifax, St. John and the West Indies. The manager of the company came to Ottawa, interviewed the Minister of Trade and Commerce and said to him. "We cannot carry on with this subsidy of $340,000. unless you allow us to raise our rates." And what do you think the Minister of Trade and Commerce did? He sent for the manager of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine which line was in competition with ithe Royal Mail Packet between Halifax and St. John and West Indian ports. These two gentlemen, the manager of the Royal Mail Packet and the manager of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine sat at the table and asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce to increase the freight rates fifty per cent, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce did it. That is the reason the rates are so high.
What year was that?

Does the hon. member
think that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine should be run at a loss when these boats are run in competition with other
