boats which have got to help pay taxes in order to carry on the merchant marine?

I do not think anything of
the kind. I am trying to prove that it is bad business to run these boats at all; and even if the rates were 50 per cent higher than they are to-day the Canadian Government Merchant Marine ships would not pay. I am trying to prove that. I say in answer to the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) that if government ships are going to be of any use to the people of the country the rates should be at least as low as the rates of any other boat, or indeed lower. But instead of that, on several occasions, they entered into an agreement with other steamship lines where they could fix the rates between the two countries. If it is good policy to have government-owned ships operate on the line between Halifax and the West Indies, why would it not be good policy to have government ships carry every pound of freight which is hauled over the National Railways in this country both East and West? Would any hon. gentleman suggest that that should be done? Is it not a fact that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine does not handle one per cent of the goods which pass over the Canadian National Railways? If the Canadian National Railways have to depend for the carriage of ninety-nine per cent of its goods by water on outside lines, and the merchant marine has lost $90,000,000, it is about time that the Canadian people woke up to the fact that they had better get clear of it.
It is also a fact that an experiment was made last year with some of those boats to cany cattle from Quebec to the Old Country, and it was found that those boats were not suitable. I am not going to blame the late government when I say that those boats are not suitable to carry cattle or to do the service that the Royal Mail Packet Company is doing to-day. I agree with the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) that the service the Royal Mail Packet Company is performing is not satisfactory. We should have fifteen-knot boats instead of ten-knot boats in order to compete with the United Fruit Company and other lines, but I say that those boats which we have at the present time are practically useless for the services to which they are devoted. What is the use of having those boats put on the West Indies route or any other route except where they are carrying bulk cargoes only in competition with other steamers? I am not complaining about the kind of boats that were built by the late government. I think everybody will admit that when the late government entered into that

policy and that contract, they never thought how they were going to use the boats. They did not know how they were going to use them. Their idea was to build as many boats as quickly as possible so that they could help during the war. I think that is a fair statement to make, and I have no hesitation in saying that when the late government, or Mr. Ballantyne, who was Minister of Marine and Fisheries at that time, brought down that policy, he had no more idea what he was going to do with the boats than any other member of the government or of the House of Commons. But the fact remains that we have them now and that there are only two things that we can do with them. We have either to go on and lose $9,000,000 every year in interest, depreciation and loss in running expenses, or to sell the boats, as somebody suggested this afternoon, and buy boats which would be suitable for this particular route. There would be no objection to that because we would not be investing any new money. I think that would be good business in view of the fact that we have some sixty of these boats which are practically useless as regards Canadian trade and which are being used to develop the trade of other countries rather than that of Canada. It would be a good policy for this government to sell some of those ships at whatever price they could get for them and, perhaps, to invest a few million dollars in building ships which would be suitable for this British West Indies route.

How does the trade of
Canada differ very much from that of any other country?

The trade of Canada differs
from that of any other country just the same as shipping differs. For instance, the trade of Canada is not at all in lumber; but the shipping of Canada, that is as regards the merchant marine, is all in one class of boats. Now, does my hon. friend see the difference? The Canadian Pacific Railway have different classes of ocean steamers. They have the regular tramp steamers for bulk cargoes, and the passenger, freight and express service by water. That is why there is a great difference, and consequently the only thing to do, if we are going to make use of the ships which we have in the Canadian Government Merchant Marine is to sell most of them and invest the money perhaps in the route between Halifax, St. John and the West Indies or some other route in order to develop trade. But I do not think it would be good business for this or any other government to spend more money in building ships for this or any other

route. There is no question that if trade should be developed by the agencies which the hon. member for Cumberland suggested, by appointing trade agents and going after the business, whenever the business is there to be handled, boats will be found to carry the products of Canada to the West Indies and to bring back to Canada the products of those islands.

What is the matter with
those ships?

As the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) said, there is nothing wrong, nothing seriously wrong with their construction. Some years ago we were told that we could not build ships in Canada, but these ships on the whole are a credit to Canada as regards their construction. The only trouble with them is that in the first place they are slow, in the second place they are all of the tramp variety, and in the third place they are not suitable for the West Indies trade or any other trade than bulk cargo. That is the only trouble with them and I think that is sufficient. It is useless for us to contend that we can get cargoes on those ships from the West Indies or anywhere else when they can travel at only between eight and ten knots an hour and when other boats from New York ports and elsewhere can travel at from eighteen to twenty knots an hour.

Does the cost of sailing
not increase very much with the rapidity of travelling? Can a slow sailing vessel carry cargo much more cheaply than a fast sailing vessel?

I do not think there is any
difference, because a Canadian Government Merchant Marine vessel will take ten or twelve days to go from Halifax to Bermuda while a fast ship will make the trip in six days, and whilst this would require more coal consumption and the capital expenditure would be a little more, that would be saved in wages, provisions and other expenses which the other boat would have to bear. Moreover, if the faster boat made the trip in half the time, she would make two trips to the other's one.
We have the merchant marine on our hands and it constitutes a white elephant. We might as well come to the conclusion that these vessels are not suitable, and as the hon. member for Cumberland said this afternoon, they have lost $265,000 each year for the last three years on operation on the West India route alone. No private company would run a business in that way. Why should the people of this country
10 p.m. have to do that just because you or I or somebody else has a quintal of fish or a barrel of flour to ship from his fish stage or his farm to some foreign country? The people of Canada should have some say in the matter and not an individual who may have something to ship, and it is suicidal for this government to go on any longer without calling a halt in the operation of most of these ships. They should sell them at once and, if necessary, get the Royal Mail Packet Company or some other company to perform this service on the West Indies route, either with or without a subsidy.

Does the hon. member
know of any place or any kind of business for which these ships are suitable?

Yes, there are many things
they can do. For instance, I understand they are used on the Pacific coast for carrying lumber. I would say they would be splendid ships for that. That is what is known as a bulk cargo. They would also be suitable for carrying coal. I understand that some of them were used on the Great Lakes for carrying wheat, but they lost money in that work. A ship, in order to carry wheat, must be specially constructed and fitted, but in order to get something for these boats to do, the management put them on the Great Lakes in the wheat-carrying business. This was a great mistake to my mind. There is no reason why those ships cannot be used for carrying bulk cargoes, and it is strange to me that in carrying bulk cargoes, they should lose money when private companies, owning ships of the same class, can make a small amount of money on the capital invested.
The hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) this afternoon said that there was a monopoly in shipping. I am afraid he has not looked into this question very thoroughly Of course there are some steamship companies which make rates; but on the Atlantic ocean where ships are going back and forth all the time from every country in "the world, there is no monopoly. Freight rates are governed entirely by the law of supply and demand except in special cases, as I said before, where vessels are given a subsidy and the Trade and Commerce department have to fix the rates with the result, as in the case of a Canadian Government Merchant Marine and the Royal Mail Packet Company, they came back to the government and the government gave them an increase of 50 per cent

That certainly is not in

It is quite true that the steamship agents in Montreal got together and made a rate for the carriage of cattle, but I am not a judge as to what they should charge for that traffic. It has been proved conclusively, however, that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine carried cattle at $20 a head and lost money; and all I am interested in is the country's investment in those ships.

A minute or two ago you
said that other companies using the same type of boat as we have in our government merchant marine were making a small profit. If that is so, there must be something wrong if our boats cannot make a profit on similar traffic.

My hon. friend should know
that boats of the type of the government merchant marine do not carry cattle, not being fitted up for the business. The boats which engage in this traffic from Montreal or Quebec are specially equipped and carry cattle in conjunction with other cargo. I did say that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine did not make any money

on the cattle business, and that is an established fact which I do not need to argue. I think it is about time that the government and the people of this country told the directors to stop operating the Canadian Government Merchant Marine.
I think we should do everything in our power to develop our trade with the West Indies, and . unless we can make a better contract either with the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company or some steamship company I feel that it is better for us to pay this subsidy than to put our own ships on the route and lose money. There is no question that our trade with the West Indies should be developed, and we in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, who are at some disadvantage in trading with the central part of Canada, have every desire to see the West Indian trade developed so that our ocean ports at St. John and Halifax will get that much more business. I do not think that taking off the ships of the government mercantile marine would tend to restrict the development of that trade, because I feel that these boats are not necessary for our National Railways at all, as the management can get all the boats necessary to handle our overseas business, and therefore I say that under the circumstances we would be able to pay the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company or some other steamship company a smaller subsidy if they had the route to themselves so that they could put on suitable boats to handle the business.
We have a heated warehouse at St. John now.

Can a boat pull in there
and unload?
Yes, and afterwards the commodities can be loaded into freight cars.

I am glad to hear it. The absence of these facilities has caused the diversion of this traffic to New York; consequently we are developing that port to the detriment of St. John and Halifax and losing the trade. I am glad to have been the first one in this House to advocate something along this line, and I am pleased to know that influential members on the government benches now see eye to eye with me; but it takes some people a long time to do so-they are just five or ten years behind the times. Last year when I discussed this matter in the House I got very little sympathy even from my own friends; they thought I was ahead of the times. But reading between the lines of what the Minister of Railways has said I know that something is going to be done and that some developments will take place in the steamship line. I am sorry the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr Duff) is not in perfect
accord with his colleagues in this matter. While the vessels of the merchant marine may not be all that is desired-may not be large enough or speedy enough-at the same time something might be done in the way of trading off two for one to bring about a development of our trade not only between Canada and the West Indies but between Canada and Mediterranean ports and other ports as well.
The hon. member for Cumberland talked about putting a duty on bananas. I talked about that myself; I advocated it, although it could do no good to me personally. I advocated it on two grounds: first, for the purpose of getting revenue. I thought there was too much direct taxation. Duties could be put on other things besides bananas without doing any harm to the country and the man in lousiness would not have to pay so much direct taxation. My second reason was in order that a preference might be given to the British West Indies. With regard to the United Fruit Company, to which reference has been made, I want to say that they are the strongest aggregation I know of in this business. Their capital must amount from seventy to a hundred million dollars. They control the steamboats; they control the plantations, and I understand that rather than ship a carload of bananas to be sold in this country at a reasonable price they will let them rot. In the early days bananas could be sold in the Canadian market at from 10 to 20 cents a dozen, but to-day you have to buy bananas in carload lots by the pound, and the average price of bananas in the Toronto market in carload lots is 7 cents a pound. So that to-day these people control the boats and the plantations; they control the bananas and they control the price, and as a result of their operations we are compelled to pay an enormous price for bananas. In other words, it is a real monopoly. That is something I hope the minister will give attention to.
What about the Combines Act?

Well, hon. members discuss the Combines Act; they condemn it, and so on, but while they do so they would like to be in a combine themselves. I would prefer to get into a combine at almost any time rather than go bankrupt. However, I will leave that to those who know more about it.
So far as lake services are concerned, there may be exorbitant rates charged. There is no doubt that during the last couple of years the rates on the lines of the Niagara Navigation Company have been very high. However,

what we have to do is to look after our own business, develop the industries of the country and develop trade between Canadian and British and foreign ports. England built up her trade by developing her merchant marine. The United States did the same thing and I contend that Canada must do the same thing. We cannot depend on private companies to do our business, because these companies are very jealous of governments or municipalities who endeavour to put on a steamboat service and every time they can get you in a corner in the matter of transportation-either a steamboat company or a railroad company- they will do it. I wish to make one or two remarks in regard to some statements of the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) concerning the merchant marine. I have never at any time stated that the larger boats in the merchant marine were a failure. I think they are good boats and should be run at a profit. The hon. member for Lunenburg said that their speed was 8 or 9 knots; the fact is their speed is 11J to 121 knots, and that is fast enough for any freight boat. The boats that are anywhere from 8,000 to 10,000 tons should be a good paying proposition for this government. As to the smaller boats, while I do not find fault with their construction, I do not think they can ever be a paying proposition. It seems to be the general habit of hon. members to criticise freight rates and then tell us about combines. If boats operated by private companies were run at a loss, hon. members would say that the owners of them were a lot of confounded fools and did not know how to carry on their business. The man who runs a steamboat ought to get a fair and reasonable price for what he carries, and should be able to make his running expenses and interest on his investment. Proof that a great many are not doing that, when it comes down to the fine point, is found in the merchant marine returns. As for railway charges. I am opposed to reducing them: I say, increase them and get our railways on a paying basis. Why should the taxpayers in a section of country that has no railway 
facilities be paying a tax so that other sections may get cheap rates? I say that the freight rates all over Canada should be equalized; then make the charges such as to enable our national railways to get on a paying basis.

I would not want this discussion to pass by without recording my attitude in regard to the proposal that has been made by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) this afternoon, especially bearing on the question of West Indian trade as set forward by the member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan). The business with the West Indies is there, waiting for transportation, waiting for the necessary arrangement between the West Indies and Canada. I do not. know that the question of the relative merit of the vessels of the present mercantile marine has any direct bearing on the question of the development of the West Indian trade with Canada. I do not suppose anyone would suggest that these vessels are especially suitable for semi-tropical trade. I think it is obvious they are not. What I understand was in the mind of the Minister of Railways was the consideration of the propriety and advisability of providing a fleet of ships such as are suitable for semitropical trade, and for carrying products of such a character as are produced in the West Indies. That is quite a different matter from the merchant marine as it is now constituted.
I do not suppose anyone would argue that we should use the merchant marine boats for this trade, because we all admit they are not ideal for that trade. In view of these three points then, Mr. Chairman-the trade being ready for us to encourage and develop, secondly, consideration of the building of ships suitable for carrying not only freight but passengers in semi-tropical areas, and thirdly, the nature of the business with the West Indies and the enormously powerful American organizations that are carrying on the trade there at the present time, I do think there is a distinct advantage in the government carrying on a business of this character. It requires a great backing, it requires wealth, it requires influence to successfully compete with the firms now operating there, and particularly with one well-known firm in the United States that has practically a monopoly of the fruit business of the West Indies.
Let me say, finally, that I hope this matter will be prosecuted with energy, that undue delay will be avoided. It certainly will appeal to the people of this country that here would

I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Cumberland, in common with the rest of the members of the House, for the splendid address that he gave us this afternoon. I think it would be in the interest of Canadian trade,
and would help to stimulate trade with the West Indian countries if that speech was published in pamphlet form and largely distributed, not only to the West Indian trade, but also to our own Canadian merchants. I do not wish to take up any time at all, except to put on record the first phase, I think I might call it, of the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite to the mercantile marine. I do not complain of the general fairness at all of the speech this afternoon of the hon. member for Lunenburg. It does not, however, present anything like a just reflection either of what took place in 1918 or in 1919, or indeed in 1920, as to the general disposition of the House towards the construction.
It will be recalled that strong pressure was brought to bear upon the government from all sides of the House for its construction, and this pressure continued right up until 1920. The resistance came first in 1921, but the resistance never took the form that it has taken now; the criticism never took that colour at all. Indeed, hon. members to my left particularly will remember just this last summer when the present Minister of Justice, then Minister of Marine and Fisheries, toured the west, he complained bitterly of the mercantile marine, and the complaint was this, that it was a war construction programme, and nothing else, and that immediately the war was over all contracts should have been cancelled. Am I mis-stating his position? If I am challenged, I will get his speech, for I have it, frequently made. Contracts should have been cancelled, he complained, when the war was over. This was the second phase of attack. Now the phase is: Oh, but you didn't build the right kind of ships; you only built bulk cargo ships. I do not pretend to be an expert upon this, but I venture to say the defence against this attack is just as effective as against any other, and I know it can be produced. I share very much the disposition apparently of hon. members to my left. A desperate struggle is being made to find something wrong with these ships, to show that they are too fast or too slow, too big or too little. The ships are all right.

As I suggested the other day in. dealing with the Railway Board, it seems to me that the government ought to try to put into practice what it has conceded in theory-that labour ought to have representation on these big public utility or government boards; that those who are actively engaged in the work- in this case the men actually engaged on the ships'-should have some voice in the management of the enterprises. There is just one other thing I should like to mention, which came up in connection with the question asked by the hon. member for Cumberland having to do with a further extension of the idea of exchange between different sections of the country. The member for Cumberland opened out a wide field, and I am quite sure that we all agree with his criticism that a great deal is lost in the transmission of commodities from one section of the country to the other. The consumer does not get the advantage that he ought to have. There are a great many commission men, and intermediaries of various kinds, that stand in the way. If we are to have our government railroads, our government steamship lines, and our government terminals it would seem a very small extension to see to it that some sort of exchange system is arranged by which a good many of the middle men that now piey on the producers could be eliminated. A few years ago some of us visited a big storage plant in the harbour of Montreal. There we saw how well equipped they were for cutting out a great many of the middleman's profits, and bringing the producer a little bit closer to the consumer. If these products of the tropics can be brought by our own ships, there is no particular reason why there could not be an almost direct exchange with the people in the West and our supplying the flour that is needed in the East. The government of New Zealand have more or less accomplished this with regard to certain kinds of dairy produce. The farmers of our own West are beginning to work in the direction of shipments through a wheat pool; and it would seem as if we would be in a position before very long to carry out this idea on an even greater scale. I would even look forward to the time when we would have not
merely our own ships plying between here and the West Indies, but also between here and the Motherland. At the same time we might very easily find that it was possible for us to carry our Canadian wheat in our own bottoms directly to the world's markets, and probably effect a direct exhange for some of the commodities we need in this country. Inevitably we are being driven into the adoption of public ownership. Whether we like it or not the world is tending in that direction. The only point we ought to safeguard is the effective control of the boards and of the operations of these corporations which are set up. I welcome the discussion this afternoon as being one of the most illuminating we have had on the floor of this House for many a long day.

Before this discussion is concluded, I crave the attention of the House for a very few moments, in order that I may put my ideas before it in regard to this question. I do not think any hon. member-I certainly would not,-would put anything in the way of a treaty agreement or any arrangement with any country or with any islands that would be for the benefit of Canada. If we can exchange the goods of our country on fair and reasonable terms, with another country, I think it is our duty so to do, A treaty whereby the products of the West Indies can be admitted on favourable terms to this country, and whereby the products of this country can be admitted on fair terms into the West Indian Islands and to the mainland of South America, would be of very great advantage to both countries. So far as Canada is concerned, I think it would be not only an advantage to the whole Dominion, but it would be especially advantageous to the Maritime provinces.
We are indebted to my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) for the valuable statistics he has given us this afternoon in connection with the trade relations or the volume of trade done with the West Indies and the possibility of an increase of trade between those islands and Canada. Of course, to carry out what is evidently in the mind of the hon. gentleman would mean a very large and comprehensive scheme and one which would be very expensive if undertaken as a whole. To my mind it would require, not one or two lines of steamers but quite a number of lines. For instance, I do not think it is a practicable proposition to undertake to trade with Cuba, if we couple it with any other island. If results are to be had with the trade or with the line of steamers running to Cuba, I maintain that these steamers must

go to that island and to that island alone. The same remark would apply to Porto Rico, to Haiti and to San Domingo. Those islands would probably require two separate lines of steamers. Then again, in order to get the trade of those islands, what arrangement can be made with our neighbours to the South of us for favourable trade agreements? I would say that inasmuch as the United States controls the trade policy of those islands to a.very large extent, Canada could not obtain any privileges there; and in that same connection I assume that when my hon. friend quoted the volume of trade between the United States and the West Indies he included the trade of Cuba and all the other islands which I have mentioned, and which are almost wholly American. We know that Cuba is a very large sugar producing country. We know that for some years past sugar has been at the top notch almost. The price has been very high indeed, and with the many millions of tons produced in that island, and with the high price of sugar per ton, the volume of trade in dollars and cents is enormous. The same thing applies to San Domingo. I do not think it applies to the same extent to Haiti or Porto Rico. In my view Canada should welcome any treaty arrangement that would assist us in capturing the trade of those islands.
So far as the steamships which have been operating are concerned, a subsidy, as hon. gentlemen know, has been paid to the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company for their services to what is called the Windward islands and Demerara. The government have also, during the last few years, been operating a service to those islands in opposition to their own subsidized service. The result is that the oompany with whom the government has a contract has not been operating a profitable service. The Minister of Trade and Commerce knows confidentially the result of the operation of that company; and if he will call to mind those results undoubtedly he will conclude that there would be no justification whatever for the government building steamers and placing them on that route. I would remind the minister of the fact that the boats operating in the present service are of very small value. Consequently the overhead- that is the insurance, depreciation and other expenses-are very small indeed as compared with the charges on four new steamers, which would be necessary to cover the route, costing probably $5,000,000. This overhead would result in a heavy loss I believe from year to year. It seems to me that the proper thing for the government to do, when they complete their treaty arrangements with our friends

to the south, is to couple up with some steamship company and pay the subsidy that is necessary to obtain the services which they will have to give under the terms of the treaty with the West Indies. To my mind that is the cheapest possible way of operating the services.
Then comes the question how far governments should interfere with vested interests. There are thousands of steamship companies operating throughout the world. I think I can safely say that scarcely one company to-day is making both ends meet, and yet some hon. gentlemen will say, without realizing what the result is going to be: Let the government build and operate those ships in competition with vested rights and private steamship companies. I think the experience we have had with the government merchant marine should be sufficient to impress the government with the fact that they cannot operate steamers in competition with private companies. I think too that the government should consider, with the money which *they have required to pay t'he losses of millions up to the present time, whether they are justified in running tonnage at a loss in opposition to private interests.
The other day I obtained the fifth annual report of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine Limited, and in running over it, I was wondering what the result in operations had been. As far as I can make out the loss has run into over $100,000,000. The statement shows, as of the 31st December, 1923, a deficit of $27,641,581. In this statement amongst the assets I find " accounts receivable, less reserve for doubtful accounts." That seems to me a rather strange entry for a steamship company which is carrying cargo and which is earning freight money, which freight money is supposed, so far as my business knowledge goes, to be payable on or before delivery of the goods. Therefore, I cannot understand why there should be accounts receivable amounting to $1,532,411. That may be a good asset or it may be a figure, a portion of which will never be realized. Then, we have as another asset, due by underwriters, claims estimated and under adjustment, $885,479. That is am asset in the account, before the deficit is struck of over $27,000,000. I will venture to say that that amount of $885,479 will show a very large shrinkage when the final settlement comes. Then there is deficiency on the other side of the account on insurance recovered. On the Canadian Exporter, one of the ships, there was a deficiency in what was estimated as the cost of the repairs. I do not know what the accident was, but on

Supply-Steamship Services
that account there was a deficiency of $23,191. Is it not reasonable to suppose that there would be a large deficiency on the $885,479? Following up this deficit of over $27,000,000, I obtained from the Department of Railways and Canals the present cost of the fleet. There are some sixty odd vessels with a tonnage of over 362,844 tons. The capital cost on 31st December, 1923, was $74,860,386.48. Add to that the loss in the operation of those boats for the last three or four years and you have a total of $102,501.968.05. The value of tonnage at the present time owned by the government is $9,724,219, leaving a shortage, if the fleet were sold to-day, of $92,777,749. That amount of $92,777,749 is based on the price of four of the ships which were sold 11 p.m. aggregating 15,508 tons. As regards the money received for them, I am perfectly sure that the credits in the figures given in the report do not provide for commissions on the sale of those boats, and the average price received for those boats works out at $26.80 a ton. I congratulate the department on obtaining such a price. It is a very outside price, and I sometimes wonder how they were able to obtain that price for those ships. But taking the 362,844 tons odd at the average price for which four of the ships have been sold, I arrive at $9,724,219 as itheir present value, leaving $92,777,749 of a shortage. Since those ships were sold at this price of $26.80 a ton, the price of ships has not increased. Not only has the price of tonnage declined but the ships are that much older, and therefore are not of so much value as when these sales were made. But even so, I venture the statement that were these boats to be sold and the account to be closed to-day, the loss to the people of Canada would be less in the long run than their continued operation. For it must be borne in mind that the country was told that these boats were to be put on new routes for developing trade, and had that been done perhaps we would have had nothing whatever to say about it, but instead they have been running the world over; in other words, they are tramp steamers. Some of my friends to my left seem to think that a steamer is simply a steamer; apparently they do not understand the difference between a tramp steamer and a steamer engaged on a regular route. These boats of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine are what are called tramps, and I undertake to say that there has been scarcely a voyage that has not resulted in loss. A government can do that; they can invest their money in railways, or steamers, or anything else, and if they
make a loss nobody is going to fail; but it is not a business proposition, it is not a proposition that any steamship-owning firm will undertake. What is the position of steamship owners in Great Britain and elsewhere at the present time? Rather than operate their tonnage at a loss, such as the government has been doing, they lay their ships up and so minimize their loss as far as possible. I should like to ask some of my friends to my left who have spoken to-night in favour of operating our present boats and building new boats to be placed in competition with private enterprise, what they would say if an agitation were started to induce the government to buy large areas of land in the West, engage in grain-growing at a loss, and sell the product at a lower price than the market value? What would our western friends say to such a proposition? Justly oppose it, of course, and bitterly. Then, why should these same people be willing, in fact insistent, that the government should spend the people's money by going into competition with privately owned steamships and vested rights? To my mind the principle is absolutely 'wrong.
Although it is expensive, in my opinion the cheapest course in the long run will be to lay these boats up and sell them as fast as possible, thus closing up the account and taking the loss. I have no criticism to make of the building of these ships. They were built at the urgent request, I believe, of the British government at a time when British shipping was being destroyed at the rate of tens of thousands of tons per week and it was feared throughout the Empire that not only our soldiers but the people of Great Britain would starve unless new tonnage was provided; therefore the construction of these ships was justified. But I cannot bring myself to believe that any government is justified in continuing to operate any such system of transportation as the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. These boats, as I said before, have not been opening up new routes for Canadian trade, they have been tramping, going down to South America and entering into competition with the regular liners there, carrying goods to Europe and thence to the United States, cutting rates and giving the benefit to foreigners, while we are paying the loss. Such kind of business should not be carried on by any government.
Does the Canadian Government Merchant Marine carry freight at a lower rate than other ocean boats?

They have, sir;
they have been carrying freight to United States ports from European ports, and from
Supply-Steamship Services

South American ports to European ports, below current rates, and at a loss-a heavy loss, $9,000,000 in one year. The Steamship companies that were running their boats on those routes were not getting remunerative rates and their yearly balances left their shareholders without any dividends.

Is it not a fact that the
Canadian Government Merchant Marine sits in at the rate conferences and abides by the rulings there made?

I am not in the confidence of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine as to what they do in that respect, but even if they ever did it only made them a little better off than they would otherwise have been and helped private interests to that extent.
But does this not show that they carried freight at the same rates as other vessels?

I think they are carrying at about the same rates as other vessels now. They go in the market, and it may be that in some cases they cut a little to secure a cargo. Now, if the government enter into the owning and operating of steamers on the West Indian route or on any other route-I mean large fast steamers-I am perfectly satisfied the result will be disastrous; there will be a deficit year by year without any very great corresponding benefit. It would be far cheaper to give a subsidy to some first class English steamship company than for the government to continue to operate their own boats at a loss.

Mr. Chairman, I congratulate
the hon. member for Cumberland on the able manner in which he dealt with the growth of trade relations with the British West Indies and other islands of the Caribbean. There was food for thought in almost every sentence, and the facts and figures that he placed on Hansard will prove both interesting and instructive to the people of this country. I have not the least doubt that the attitude of some of the people of this country toward the operation of a steamship service between Canada and the West Indies in connection with the Canadian National Railway system will at least be greatly changed. I am not at this late hour going to enter upon any detailed argument or any elaboration of facts in connection with the matters that were so well put before the committee by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Ixigan) but those facts are sufficient to prove conclusively that there are great possibilities of growth 
of trade between Canada and the West Indies. When Sir Charles Tupper was in England endeavouring to counteract a movement on the part of the Hon. Joseph Howe to bring about a repeal of the union, he said to John Bright that if the union were displaced the greater part of eastern Canada would go into the United States. John Bright replied:
I cannot help thinking that it would be a good thing to see one government from the equator to the north pole.
Now, Sir, that day has passed. Canada is a nation extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and the idea of one government from the equator to the north pole can be carried out by including the West Indies in a free trade relation with Canada in order that we may be able to import into this country, as the hon. member for Cumberland said this afternoon, these tropical products which alone we lack to make us an independent nation in the sense of our having everything which is necessary for the life and comfort and needs of our people. That being the case, why should the government not address itself to the question of bringing about better trade relations with the West Indies and to that end establish a steamship service operated by the Canadian National Railway system that would be efficient in point of speed, passenger accommodation, cold storage and general freight capacity, a service that would cause trade to flow through Canadian channels rather than be sent through the United States ports by the steamers of the United Fruit Company?
I do not take the pessimistic view of the hon. member for King's, P.E.I. (Mr. Hughes) when he says that the Maritime provinces can never succeed industrially. The opening of the Panama canal has given us a great opportunity of carrying on water-borne traffic with the great province of British Columbia and, by rail, with Saskatchewan and Alberta. We have all the natural resources; we have the coal, we have the iron, we have the steel, and we have in Nova Scotia undeveloped water powers sufficient to enable us, with cheap transportation through the Panama canal, to compete with central Canada for the industrial business of British Columbia and some portions of Saskatchewan and Alberta. If that is true, then the pessimism of the hon. member for King's, P.E.I. in reference to the industrial future of the Maritime provinces is not quite to the point.
It seems to me that a red herring was drawn across the trail by hon. members during the discussion this afternoon and this evening by holding up the bugbear of the

Canadian merchant marine. The Canadian merchant marine was constructed during the war period and the years immediately succeeding the war. They were built with no objective as to the trade they were to enter; they were built for the purpose of carrying in the best possible way whatever was to be taken across the ocean, and they had to be built in the quickest possible time. If direct steamship connection with the West Indies in connection with the Canadian National Railway system is not to be had because of the failure of the Canadian merchant marine, then I submit we had better scrap it. We had better put that history behind us so that the future of Canada in its trade with the West
Indies or with any other part of the Empire shall not be hampered or interfered with through the failure of the merchant marine to pay its way.
Let us look for a moment at the figures. The minister is asking for an appropriation of $340,000 for the steamship service between Halifax and St. John and the West Indies operated by the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company. The hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Black) knows these ships and how they are operated; it is his company in the city of Halifax that are the operators of them to a certain extent. He knows that one of these ships was lost off Bermuda some months ago and that the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company put in the service an inferior boat, a boat that does not carry passengers and does not conform to the requirements. The company are operating better ships on other lines, whereas the service given between Canada and the West Indies
does not come up to what the contract calls for. The hon. member has rathei damned with faint praise the suggestion ol the hon. member for Cumberland and the statement of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham). He has held up the Canadian merchant marine as a nightmare to the Canadian people. We have to-day, Sir, 23,,000 miles of railway operated by Sir Henry Thornton and his board, of directors. That railway system has cost this country $1,386,000,000. We are told that these railways are the great feeders, the great conductors, the great centralizers of export and import trade,yet it is said that we should not have connected with these railways up-to-dlate steamship services in order that they may carry the traffic originating in foreign countries as well as in our own.
I think the minute the government decide to have the Canadian National Railways operate a steamship line to the West Indies they should get away from the name "Canadian Government Merchant Marine." Let
Supply-Steamship Services
that be something that is to be forgotten, and let the service be called the Canadian National Ocean Steamship Company, Limited. Let the ships be up to date, modern in every particular, capable of meeting the needs of the merchants of the West Indies and of Canada in that trade. If we take the subsidy of $340,000 and the deficit of last year on the Canadian Government Merchant Marine of $265,000, we get a total of $605,000. That is what this country is paying every year for its West India service. In ten years that is $6,050,000. Take the West Indian agreement, whereby the British West India islands agree when a new weekly service is inaugurated by Canada to pay $135,000 as their proportion of the subsidy. That means $740,000 a year, or $7,400,000 in ten years. I have it on good authority that four ships of modern type, of 12 knots, with passenger, freight and cold storage accommodation. can be built for $1,000,000 apiece; that is $4,000,000, and you have $7,400,000, which means that they will much more than pay for themselves in ten years. If this is a business proposition, then why should we have obsolete boats, to use the words of the junior member for Halifax? He said these boats of the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company could be operated much miore cheaply than boats to be built by the government, and the reasons he gave were that they were of small value, which means poor boats, that the insurance rate was low, and the depreciation not very great. He estimated four new ships would cost $5,000,000. Taking his figures, and giving him the benefit of the doubt, say these four ships of the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company are worth $3,000,000, then this government and this country are paying the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company on their investment nearly 12 per cent; 12 per cent would be $360,000, and we are giving them $340,000.
I say that these facts give food for thought. It is a matter that should be approached carefully, wisely and cautiously. I think, as was foreshadowed by the Minister of Railways this afternoon, that during the vacation the Railway department, together with the Trade and Commerce department and the business men of the Maritime provinces and other parts of Canada and of the West Indies, should get together in order to see how the trade relation could be benefited and strengthened, and how a better steamship service could be obtained.. If it can be obtained in the way that was outlined by my hon. friend from Cumberland this afternoon, and which was intimated by the Minister

Supply-Steamship Services

of Railways as the probable policy of the government, I think it would meet with the hearty approval not only of hon. gentlemen in this House, but of the country generally. We in the Maritime provinces are practically dying of ennui, and if we cannot build up our export and our import trade, if we cannot send the products of the Maritime provinces to the West Indies and bring back to Canada their tropical fruits and other products, then our last hope is gone. I remember as a boy the sailing fleets that used to go out of my home port, Halifax. There was the hum of industry and the din of traffic at that port then, and I tell you that to-day if it was not for the Canadian National Railway system, and the wise policy of Sir Henry Thornton, Halifax, would not be on the map as a port at all.
Speaking about the Canadian National and the operation of steamships, Sir Henry Thornton entered into an agreement with the Cunard and the White Star Steamship Companies this last winter, as a result of which he brought more tonnage and shipping to the extent of one million tons, to the port of Halifax in five months than came in during *the previous year, and instead of bringing eleven thousand people to the port of Halifax in those five months, to be taken over the Canadian National, he brought twenty-eight thousand, or over 112i per cent more. He sent his agents abroad, he had his steamship connections, and he got the business for his own railway lines. Now if he can do that with steamship companies that are independent of this government, if he has the foresight and the wisdom to work out a solution in conjunction with steamship companies not a part of his system, what could he not do if he was given reasonable latitude in developing an ocean steamship policy with modern up-to-date boats, to be operated in conjunction with the Canadian National Railway system. Who objects to that? Is there any shareholder of the Canadian Pacific who objects to that company operating their own steamship services? Look at their fleets of magnificent steamers, operating across practically every ocean in the wide world.
But my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax says:	Oh, that is private ownership,
and the other is government ownership. My hon. friend knows as well as I do that the Canadian National Railway system is operated by a private company, of which Sir Henry Thornton is the president, free from government control, free from parliamentary control outside of the estimates that are necessary to

give him the money wherewith to carry on. If that is so, we should not as hon. members of this House allow our judgment to be warped because of private interests. We should stand for the public interest, as the public interest requires public men to do.
I can see the Halifax Herald. Of a few weeks ago, with blazing headlines, "Mr. Black Returning to Ottawa to Look After The Interests Of The Port Of Halifax." I hope, Mr. Chairman, that they will read Hansard to-morrow and see the faint praise that he gave the hon. member for Cumberland who is trying to build up a trade for the Maritime ports and help the people of the Maritime provinces by putting on a steamship line that would meet with the approval of our people, and make our hearts glad to see them coming into the ports of Halifax and St. John. He damned that proposal with faint praise because his duty, first, was not to the port of Halifax, but as I conceive it, to the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company, of which he and his company, Pickford and Black, Limited, are the managers and the operators at the port of Halifax to-day.

I just want to say a few words, Mr. Chairman, before the item carries. I have listened with a great deal of pleasure and deep interest to members on both sides of the House who have spoken on this subject of the development of bur trade with the West Indies. I wish to join with other members of the House in congratulating the hon. member for Cumberland on his masterly presentation to the House this afternoon. It was one of the most informative, eloquent and constructive trade discussions to which it has been my pleasure to listen in this House.
I want to say just a few words in reference to the remarks of the right hon. leader of the opposition. He has apparently come to the conclusion that the members on this side of the House have changed their opinion of the merchant marine. He spoke of their vicious opposition to it as a reckless expenditure. I can only say to my right hon. friend that if any groups of men in this House were to propose the same plan, or the same scheme, I think that every hon. member on this side would oppose it just as vigorously as hon. members did on that occasion.
They did not oppose it at all.

I am using the words of my
right hon. friend. I may be mistaken, but I took his words down.

Supply-Steamship Services
That was after the construction was practically complete.

I think I took down my
right hon. friend's exact words.
That is right but it was after the construction was practically complete.

The real difficulty is that the
ships were not designed properly for the work they were to perform. The whole scheme was very ill-considered, and I am sure that if this government were to attempt to build vessels according to any such ill-considered plan as that of my right hon. friend many members of the House would oppose it. The junior member for Halifax (Mr. Black) said he did not think that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine could compete with other lines. In that I agree with him at the present. But what is the real cause of this? The reason is obvious. The ships are not designed or built for the purposes of trade between the West Indies and Canadian ports. I venture to say, however, that if the shrewd president of the Canadian National Railways undertakes to build ships and place a service upon that route he will do so in exactly the same manner as the Canadian Pacific Railway would1 do if they were undertaking such a service.

The same way as the
" Palais Canadien " was acquired?

There is only one thing more I want to say in reference to a statement by the minister; I know he made it inadvertently. I want to warn him against putting his foot in a very bad and deepr hole. He is anxious to foster trade, but the only specific suggestion he made was that we might adopt the system of having consular trade agents similar to that which the United States follows, and having those trade agents remunerated by fees, or largely by fees, on export invoices. That appeals apparently to the minister. My warning is this:	That
he should look up the debate of 1921. In that year we brought into parliament this proposal. It met with fierce opposition from his friends. My hon. friend was not in the House at the time. My recollection of its fate is that it passed this House, but that his government abandoned it. I would not like him now bo commit himself too closely to a programme which was so treated at the hands of his party.

I did not say that I was
strongly in favour of it. I merely said the plap was worth considering.

Worth re-considering
put it.

No, worth considering.
Supply-Steamship Services

I would put it, worth
re-considering.

Item agreed to.
Canada and South Africa, steamship service between, $125,000.

Are we to sit until after midnight? We have taken up time to-day which has been pretty well distributed. We have no nights now at all. We are sitting late every night, and it is nearly midnight again.

The summer is coming and
we would like to get through as soon as possible. I think we might proceed for a little while longer. I may say this item has been reduced by $21,000.
What company is giving the service?

It is the Elder Dempster
Company with offices in Montreal.

Is it the same service
as before?
Yes.

How many trips a year
are given?
Eleven trips a year.

St. John or Montreal?
Mr. LOW7:	Montreal in the summer time
and St. John in the winter time.

Item agreed to.
Canada and New Zealand on the Pacific ocean, steam sendee between, $100,000.

Is this the same service
as before?
Yes.
How many trips a year?
Twelve trips.
What goods are carried?

I,umber is one of the large
items.
Mr, MEIGHEN:	Seeing that the merchant marine boats are practically only fitted for lumber, according to the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff), how is it that one of our own boats does not run on this service?
The articles carried are: Canned salmon, fresh fruit, potatoes, onions, leather, rubber boots, lumber, codfish, whiskey, bicycles, chairs, horses, suspenders, sewing machines, hardware and machinery.

The minister knows that the boats of the merchant marine can carry

that class of freight all right, and it is practically all lumber anyway. Why has he not a merchant marine boat on this service, if he believes what his friends have been arguing all day?

This is a passenger and mail
service, as well as freight.
The minister said nearly all lumber.

Freight is carried in addition
to the passenger and mail service.
What Company is the contract made with?
The Union Steamship Company of New Zealand. New Zealand contributes $100,000 and the Fiji government about $25,000.

Do we bonus boats to
carry passengers?

No, but my hon. friend asked
me why the merchant marime could not operate this service, and I replied that it was a passenger service as well as a freight service.

I know, but we are not interested as a government in the passenger end; we are interested in the freight end, to get sale for our goods. The goods we sell can go on the merchant marine boats. If what the government says about these boats is correct, they should be on this service.

I doubt very much whether
it would be possible to make it pay with the freight service alone.

I doubt very .much if
there is much else. We have not much passenger business to New Zealand. That business would not sustain anything at all.

There is a passenger traffic
through Canada en route to England, and there is a passenger service as well to Australia.
It goes to Australia?

Yes. We do not subsidize it
to Australia.

There might be a very
little service to England, but there are other boats to perform that service. I think if the minister will wait till morning he will find out that our boats will not carry lumber. That is usually the verdict. There is always something else they will not carry.

Perhaps not. My hon. friend
knows better than I do about that.

Item agreed to.

Supply-Steamship Services
Prince Rupert, B.C., and Queen Charlotte islands, steam service between, $21,000.
Are these yearly contracts?
This contract is for three years. It was made last year.

Are there any boats
carrying grain out of Prince Rupert?
-Not that I know of-no elevators out there.

Where does the minister
expect to get the boats when the new elevator is put up for the Prince Rupert route?

I am sure there are many
vessels that will be glad to go into Prince Rupert if they can get a cargo.

And around by the
Panama canal?

I do not know what route they
will follow. They will follow the route which will be to the best advantage.

Would the Panama not
be the only route?

It would depend on where
they were going.
But for grain.
There is a trade developed with the Orient.

Item agreed to.
Victoria and San Francisco, steam service between, $3,000.	'

I do not think this item is
debatable. We are compelled by the order an council pursuant to the British North American Act admitting British Columbia to confederation to keep up this service.

Item agreed to.
Victoria, Vancouver, way ports and Skagway, steam service between, $25,000.
What company is that?
Is this under the British ,North America Act?

The item just passed, the
Victoria and Sam Francisco service is the one to which I referred. If my right hon. friend has any doubt, that the order is pursuant to the British North America Act I will read the clause to him. It is as follows:
The Dominion will provide an efficient mail service fortnightly by steam communication between Victoria and San Francisco and twice a week between Victoria and Olympia, the vessels to be adapted for the conveyance ol freight and passengers.
That is a clause in the order in council pursuant to the British North America Act, admitting British Columbia to confederation.

Then my answer was
right.

What company operates
this service?

The Caifcidian Pacific Railway
Company operates this Victoria-Skagway service.

Is there a suggestion that
the Canadian. Government Merchant Marine should enter into the service or the Canadian National? I understand they are looking for a steamer; they wish to have one built or buy one to put on this service?
I have no knowledge of it.
Will this pay for the cost of carrying the mail.

Yes, any boat we subsidize is
compelled to carry mail.

Item agreed to.
Vancouver and Northern ports of British Columbia steam service between, $24,800.

What company has that
contract?
The Union Steamship Company of British Columbia.
Item agreed to.
The minister is not going to ask us to deal with the other items tonight.

I would like to make a little
progress.

You have made a lot
of progress.
Let us proceed a little further.

Some hon. gentlemen
may want to discuss these items.

I do not want to press the
matter, but I want to make progress.
You have made progress.
I do not think so.

I do not think you
will make any progress by pressing it further to-night.

If there is any special item
my hon. friend wishes to have stand over, I am quite agreeable.
Postal Employees
We have not obstructed anything to-night.

Let us take the items to the
bottom of the page; they are only small ones.

There may be some
discussion, and you have done very well. Any delay. which has -occurred to-day has been on the debate brought about by an hon. member on the minister's side of the House. Why should he press the House further?

Then I will stop for to-night.
